feedback.problem:
What is the smallest possible distance between the points $(b,2b)$ and $(3,0),$ where $b$ is a real number? Do not round the answer.

The smallest possible distance is
{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the *squared* distance $S(b)$ between the two points. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}S(b) & ={(b-3)}^{2}+{(2b-0)}^{2} \\  & =(b-3)^{2}+(2b)^{2} \\  & =({b}^{2}-6b+9)+(4{b}^{2}) \\  & =5{b}^{2}-6b+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want to minimize $S,$ we compute the derivative ${S}^{′}(b).$ This gives

$$
{S}^{′}(b)=10b-6.
$$

The stationary points of $S(b)$ are the points where the derivative ${S}^{′}(b)=0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(b) & =0 \\ 10b-6 & =0 \\ b & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}\,(\frac{3}{5})=10>0.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $b=\frac{3}{5}.$ 

Since $S(b)$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $b=\frac{3}{5}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{5})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{5})} \\  & =\sqrt{5{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}-6(\frac{3}{5})+9} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{5}-\frac{18}{5}+9} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36}{5}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{6\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the smallest possible distance between the points $(b,2b)$ and $(3,0)$ is $\frac{6\sqrt{5}}{5}.$
